paragraphs.heading: The basic form
paragraphs.text: A linear equation is one that can be written in the form a₁x₁ + … + aₙₓₙ + b = 0. The x's are the variables, also called unknowns, and the a's and b are the coefficients, which are often real numbers. The coefficients can be any expressions at all, as long as none of the variables appears in them. For the equation to mean something, a₁, …, aₙ cannot all be zero. The lone coefficient b is known as the constant term.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a solution
paragraphs.text: A solution is a choice of values that makes the equation true when you put them in place of the unknowns. With just one variable there is exactly one solution, as long as a₁ ≠ 0. People often mean this one-variable case when they say "linear equation", and then the variable is fittingly called the unknown.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is called linear
paragraphs.text: With two variables x and y, the equation takes the form ax + by + c = 0, with at least one of a and b nonzero. Each solution is a pair of numbers you can read as the coordinates of a point in the plane. If a and b are real numbers there are infinitely many solutions, and together they make a line. Every line, in turn, is the full set of solutions of such an equation, and this match between lines and equations is where the name linear comes from.

paragraphs.heading: Slopes and special lines
paragraphs.text: When b ≠ 0, you get the graph of a function of x: its line has y-intercept − c/b and slope − a/b. If b = 0, the line is vertical, with equation x = −c/a, and it is not the graph of a function of x. In the same way, if a = 0 the line is horizontal, with equation y = −c/b.

paragraphs.heading: Linear or affine
paragraphs.text: The word linear can mislead. In calculus, a function whose graph is a line is usually called linear. In linear algebra, though, a linear function is one that sends a sum to the sum of the images of its parts, and the function above passes that test only when c = 0, so its line goes through the origin. To avoid the clash, functions whose graph is any line are often called affine functions, and the ones with c = 0 are called linear maps.

paragraphs.heading: More variables, more uses
paragraphs.text: With n variables, the solutions form a hyperplane, which is a subspace of dimension n − 1 inside n-dimensional Euclidean space. Linear equations appear throughout mathematics and in its uses in physics and engineering. Part of the reason is that non-linear systems can often be approximated well by linear equations.
